schema_a.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests
schema_a.talk_title: Statistical considerations for early cancer detection test performance
schema_a.MOA_summary: Bob Smith explained that sensitivity and specificity for single-cancer early detection tests differ from multi-cancer tests, highlighted the concept of program sensitivity, and argued that MCEDs have lower aggregate sensitivity but broader public health impact, emphasizing the need for contextual interpretation of performance metrics.
key_findings: Program sensitivity can equalize comparisons between frequent low-cost tests and less frequent high-cost tests.
Sensitivity and specificity can move together when test quality improves, contrary to the assumed inverse relationship.
MCED aggregate sensitivity is lower than single-cancer tests, but modeling suggests annual MCED screening could prevent 17% of cancer deaths.
Stage shift is a blunt endpoint; within-stage tumor size changes can drive survival benefits.
False positive rates for MCEDs are often mischaracterized; a 1% rate reflects the complement of PPV at biopsy.

schema_a.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests
schema_a.talk_title: Defining target condition and cancer signal origin in MCED tests
schema_a.MOA_summary: Nima Visvade argued that the target condition for MCEDs should be defined by clinically actionable cancer signal origin (CSO), emphasizing biologic parity and diagnostic pathway grouping to improve workup efficiency and clinical utility.
key_findings: Target condition for MCEDs is inseparable from cancer signal origin, which guides diagnostic pathways.
Methylation‑based MCEDs provide accurate CSO predictions that are clinically useful for directing workup.
Biologic families (e.g., HPV‑related tumors) may be more appropriate grouping than strict organ boundaries.
Pathway‑based grouping aligns workup burden with clinical benefit, allowing a single imaging study to evaluate multiple CSOs.
High CSO accuracy transforms MCEDs from vague screening signals to actionable diagnostic starting points.

schema_a.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests
schema_a.talk_title: Generalizability and implementation considerations for MCED and single‑cancer tests
schema_a.MOA_summary: Asma Shukat highlighted how trial enrichment (age, stage, risk) inflates performance metrics of early detection tests and advocated for age‑sex adjustment, detailed subgroup reporting, and likelihood ratios to improve generalizability to real‑world populations.
key_findings: Trial populations often enrich for older age, higher stage, or known cancers, leading to inflated sensitivity and PPV.
Healthy‑volunteer bias can produce lower prevalence than intended use, underestimating PPV.
Age and sex standardization to the US census modestly shifts sensitivity and specificity, as shown in the PREEMPT CRC cohort.
Granular reporting of performance by cancer type, stage, lesion size, and advanced precursor lesion subcategories is needed but limited by power.
Likelihood ratios and number‑needed‑to‑screen are valuable metrics for clinicians to assess post‑test probability.

talk_metadata.talk_title: Translating clinical trial data into intended use populations
rhetorical_signals: Speaker said: "Our trials are very often biased on purpose because we need to get a certain number of cases of cancer"
Speaker said: "When you look at a test that goes into a population that has a different makeup than what the trial population was"

vulnerability_identified.mechanistic_blindspot: Enrichment with high‑risk or advanced‑stage cancers inflates sensitivity and PPV

trial_dilution_risk.flawed_enrollment_criteria: Over‑representation of 50‑54 year olds and women, under‑representation of >75 year olds
trial_dilution_risk.missing_biomarker: Age‑adjusted prevalence weighting not applied in primary analysis
trial_dilution_risk.statistical_concern: Sensitivity and specificity shift after age/sex adjustment

key_data_gaps: Lack of real‑world validation of adjusted performance metrics

crispro_opportunity.description: Incorporate age‑sex standardization prospectively in trial protocols to avoid post‑hoc adjustments.
crispro_opportunity.transcript_evidence: Speaker said: "We adjusted it, and then we said, 'Okay, how does the performance of the test change?'"
crispro_opportunity.crispro_angle: CrisPRO can simulate population distributions to guide enrollment quotas before trial launch.

crispro_opportunity.description: Report sensitivity by lesion size and histology within each stage to refine performance estimates.
crispro_opportunity.transcript_evidence: Speaker said: "Not all stage one cancers are created equal... size of the tumor correlates with how much it's shed"
crispro_opportunity.crispro_angle: CrisPRO can model shedding dynamics as a function of tumor volume and histologic subtype.
